idiom_name: hand-written lightweight implementation of the collaborator interface over an in-memory store
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: implement the depended-on component's services in a test-only type whose state lives in an in-memory container (hash table, map, list), and keep the interaction self-consistent - values written by earlier calls are returned by later calls. Do not configure expectations or canned answers: working behaviour is what separates a fake from a test stub or mock. Install it through the substitutable dependency the system under test supports (constructor or parameter injection, factory, registry, test-specific subclass), re-create or clear it for every test, and grow it only to cover the services the current tests actually use. Where the language or ecosystem already ships a faithful in-memory subsystem (embedded database, in-memory file system, in-process server), prefer it over a hand-rolled store. Keep at least one test against the real component so drift is detected.
code_sketch:
repo = in_memory_repo()                      # implements the DOC's interface over a hash table
sut = SystemUnderTest(repo)                  # installed through the substitutable dependency
sut.create_user('ada')                       # writes land in the fake's store
assert sut.get_user('ada').name == 'ada'     # later reads see the earlier writes
# no expectations configured: the fake has working behaviour, not canned answers
pitfalls: Configuring the fake with expectations or per-test canned answers turns it into a stub or mock; the working behaviour is the point.
Sharing one fake instance across tests through static or module-level state makes failures order-dependent.
Letting the fake grow without a test against the real component leaves the suite validating a simplified, silently diverging contract.

Wrong move: using an in-memory database fake (H2, SQLite, EF Core InMemory) as the only test of persistence code -> tests stay green while the real engine rejects data (native enums, unenforced foreign keys, dialect-specific SQL) -> instead keep the fake for unit tests only and cover the contract with integration tests against the real engine, e.g. via Testcontainers.

Wrong move: letting the fake absorb behaviour until it is a full re-implementation of the real component -> every real-component change must be mirrored twice and the suite certifies the fake's semantics -> instead cap the fake at the services current tests use, or replace it with an embedded/containerised real component.

Wrong move: modelling only the fake's happy path because failure modes are harder to write -> error handling, constraint violations and rollback logic are never exercised and break on first real failure -> instead make the fake able to simulate the real component's failures (configurable errors, latency) or keep integration tests for them.
sources: Gerard Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns: Refactoring Test Code (Addison-Wesley, 2007) - Fake Object (Test Double Patterns, Chapter 23), variations: Fake Database, In-Memory Database, Fake Web Service, Fake Service Layer.
Martin Fowler, Test Double (Bliki, 2007) - Fake definition: 'has a working but simplified implementation', clarifying Fake's place in the Meszaros taxonomy alongside Dummy, Stub, Spy and Mock.

Martin Fowler, Mocks Aren't Stubs (2007) - Distinguishes mockist vs. classicist TDD and clarifies that Fake sits between Stub (canned state) and Mock (expectation-based verification) by providing working but simplified behaviour.
